intuition: A right rotation moves the last k values in front of the rest. Reverse the entire array, then reverse each of those two parts. The first reversal moves the parts; the next two restore their internal order. Reduce k by the array length because full-length rotations change nothing.

Let A be the first n-k values and B the final k values. The desired result is B followed by A. Reversing the whole array gives reverse(B) followed by reverse(A), so reversing those two segments separately restores their internal order while retaining their swapped positions.

Normalize k modulo n because n right shifts return every value to its original position. Each reversal swaps endpoint values while moving its pointers inward, without allocating slices. The three passes modify the same list, and the method’s output is the mutation rather than a newly returned rotated array.

steps: For nums=[1,2,3,4,5,6,7] and k=3, modulo reduction leaves k=3 and divides the original into A=[1,2,3,4], B=[5,6,7].
Reverse the full list to obtain [7,6,5,4,3,2,1], with reversed B before reversed A.
Reverse indices 0 through 2. The first segment becomes [5,6,7], producing [5,6,7,4,3,2,1].
Reverse indices 3 through 6 to restore [1,2,3,4] in the second segment.
The original list now contains [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. That mutation is the three-position right rotation; no separate result list is created.

codeNotes.note: Full-length rotations are identity operations. Reducing k also ensures the two segment boundaries remain valid even when the requested shift exceeds n.
Swapping inward endpoints reverses a segment in the original list, using constant extra space rather than creating copied slices.
After the whole-list and first-segment reversals, this final pass restores the original order of A behind the already restored segment B.

keyDecision: After reducing k modulo n, reverse the whole array, then 0..k - 1, then k..n - 1.

concept.question: Why do three reversals move the final block forward without reversing its final order?
intuition: Shifting one position repeatedly takes too much work for large rotation counts. A right rotation swaps two blocks while preserving the order inside each.

Call the prefix block A and the final requested-count block B. Reversing the whole array gives reversed B followed by reversed A. Reversing those two segments separately restores each block’s internal order, leaving B followed by A.
concept.observation: Reduce the rotation count by full array-length revolutions before splitting the blocks.
approach: Reduce the requested right shift modulo array length.
Reverse the moved front block and the remaining back block separately.
concept.correctness: Every nontrivial rotation splits the sequence into A followed by B, with desired result B followed by A. Reversing the whole sequence yields reversed B followed by reversed A. Reversing each segment is its own inverse, so the next two reversals yield exactly B followed by A, preserving every original occurrence.

complexity.explanation: The three reversals swap only a linear number of pairs in the original array. Time is linear and the endpoint references and swaps use constant auxiliary storage.

pitfalls: Reduce the rotation count by full array-length revolutions before splitting the blocks.
Apply the right-rotation split after reducing the count.
